title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
publisher: Mind, vol. 59, no. 236, Oxford University Press
pitch: The paper that asked 'Can machines think?' and proposed the imitation game, now called the Turing test. It ends with a plan for learning machines.

chapters.g: Turing replaces 'Can machines think?' with a test: can a machine pass as a human in a text conversation?
Why this test is a fair way to frame the question.

chapters.t: The Machines concerned in the Game

chapters.g: How a digital computer works: store, executive unit and control.
One digital computer can imitate any other, given enough memory and time.

chapters.t: Contrary Views on the Main Question
chapters.g: Turing answers nine objections, from theological to 'Lady Lovelace's objection' that machines only do what they are told.
Instead of programming an adult mind, build a child machine and teach it. A preview of machine learning.

ideas: Learning machines may be the way to intelligence.

args.a: If a machine behaves intelligently, we should say it thinks.
args.c: John Searle's Chinese Room and others argue behaviour is not the same as understanding.

questions: Do today's chatbots pass Turing's test? Does that mean they think?
Which of the nine objections is strongest today?

quiz.q: What did Turing call his test?
quiz.w: We now call it the Turing test.

o: Machines can only do what we tell them
quiz.w: Turing replies that machines can surprise us.
